Almost everything in this course follows one blueprint. Start with a population, draw one sample, calculate a statistic, then ask: if we drew sample after sample, where would all those statistics land? This simulator lets you do that yourself.

Press **+1** to draw a sample, then **+50** or **+500** to draw many. Click any dot to see the sample behind it. Change the population, the sample size or the true effect and draw again.

## Things to try

Each link opens the simulator ready to go. Before you press a button, predict what will happen.

### Why does a bigger sample help?

- [Means of 5 observations](../simulator/index.html?step=2&n=5&view=raw&draws=500). Panels 1 and 3 share the same axis, so compare how far the means spread with how far the scores spread. Then move the slider to 25 and draw again.
- Compare the **SD of M** in the table with the true standard error, σ / √n. The standard error is the SD of all those sample means.

### Does the scale of the test matter?

- [A test with mean 500 and SD 100](../simulator/index.html?step=2&n=10&mu=500&sd=100&view=raw&draws=500). The means are on a new scale. Now set "Show the statistic as" to z. How does this compare with a test that has mean 100 and SD 15, or a GPA with mean 3 and SD 0.5? Type those values in to check.

### Why do gains help?

- [Before and after](../simulator/index.html?step=3p&n=15&d=0.4&draws=800). Each line in panel 2 is one person. Note how often we reject H₀. Then raise the correlation of before and after: the mean gain stays the same, but the gains get steadier, and rejections become more common.

### Does the population have to be normal?

- [Means from a skewed population](../simulator/index.html?step=2&n=2&pop=rightskew&view=raw&draws=500). With n = 2 the means are still skewed. Raise n to 30 and draw again. This is the central limit theorem.

### Why do we divide by n − 1?

- [Samples of 5](../simulator/index.html?step=2&n=5&draws=2000). In the table, compare **SS / n** with **σ̂²**, and both with the true σ² of 225. Dividing by n falls short on average, and dividing by n − 1 lands on target. Then click a few dots: in some samples, SS / n overshoots.
- Also look at **σ̂**. Even when σ̂² is right on average, its square root runs a little low.

### Why do we need the t-distribution?

- [z with the true σ](../simulator/index.html?step=2&n=5&draws=2000). About 5% of samples land beyond ±1.96.
- [t with the estimate σ̂](../simulator/index.html?step=3&n=5&draws=2000). Same samples, but now we use an estimate, so the t cutoffs sit farther out. Look at **Beyond ±1.96** in the table: that's how often the old z cutoffs would mislead us. Then raise n and watch the problem fade.

### What does a p-value look like?

- [Five percent of the time, by chance](../simulator/index.html?step=4&n=20&draws=1000). There is no effect here, yet about 5% of samples look significant. Those are Type I errors.
- [A real effect](../simulator/index.html?step=4&n=20&d=0.5&draws=1000). Now the share beyond the cutoffs is the power.

### Why is ANOVA a ratio of variances?

- [No group differences](../simulator/index.html?step=5&n=10&draws=2000). Compare **MS within** and **MS between** in the table. Both estimate σ², so F hovers around 1.
- [Real group differences](../simulator/index.html?step=5&n=10&d=1&draws=2000). MS within stays where it was, MS between grows, and F moves right.
- [Only one group differs](../simulator/index.html?step=5&n=10&gm=100,100,115&draws=2000). Type your own group means to try other patterns. F says that the means differ, but not which ones.

### How do correlation and regression relate?

- [A slope with n = 20](../simulator/index.html?step=7&n=20&d=0.4&draws=800). Each dot is one estimate b. The table compares the average a and b with the true intercept and slope. The intercept is where the line meets X = 0, so try a different true intercept: the line moves, and the slope doesn't.
- [A yes/no predictor](../simulator/index.html?step=7b&n=20&d=0.5&draws=800). With a yes/no X, the slope is just the difference between two group means, and its t is the t from a two-sample test.
- [Drag the points](../simulator/index.html?tab=correlation&r=0.6&n=12&resid=1). Pull one point far away, and see what happens to the line, r and the residuals. Then try it [with many points](../simulator/index.html?tab=correlation&r=0.6&n=200).

### What does a confidence interval promise?

- [100 intervals](../simulator/index.html?tab=intervals&n=10&draws=100). The population mean never moves. The intervals do. About 95% of them catch it. Then raise n and watch them narrow.
- [When H₀ is false](../simulator/index.html?tab=intervals&n=10&d=0.89&draws=100). An interval that leaves out the H₀ mean means the same as rejecting H₀. Look at how often that happens, then compare it with the power for the same effect and sample size.

### What gives a study power?

- [Four levers](../simulator/index.html?tab=power&d=0.89&n=10). Start at 80% power, then change alpha, the test, the sample size and the effect size one at a time.

## Credit

This simulator was written for EDUC 15. It was inspired by the visualizations of Kristoffer Magnusson at [R Psychologist](https://rpsychologist.com/viz/), including [p-values](https://rpsychologist.com/pvalue/), [statistical power](https://rpsychologist.com/d3/NHST/), [confidence intervals](https://rpsychologist.com/d3/CI/) and [correlation](https://rpsychologist.com/correlation/). They're well worth exploring too.
